summary: Ground Check is an interactive map that helps the people of Tuktoyaktuk, NWT, see which land could host a new town site, as coastal erosion and storm flooding push the community to consider relocating. Residents have said they can’t choose a site without seeing it on a map. Ground Check splits about 200 km² of land along the Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk Highway into 3,578 squares of 240 m and gives each one measured values. These are height, distance from the shore and how far that shore has moved, distance to the highway and town, nearby lakes, radar-measured summer ground movement, and whether it stays dry in published 2020–2100 storm-flood scenarios. Residents set their own rules, for example “high ground within 15 km of town that stays dry in a 1-in-100-year storm in 2100”. They instantly see which places fit, and why others don’t. Nothing is ranked or scored, and every place still needs a drilled core before building. A second view, for researchers, automatically checks every new NASA–ISRO NISAR radar pass over Tuk. It shows, pair by pair, how well NISAR measures the ground compared with Sentinel-1, building toward the first validated thaw season in summer 2027.
details:
What it does: Ground Check is an interactive map that helps the people of Tuktoyaktuk, NWT, see which land could host a new town site. Coastal erosion and storm flooding are pushing the community to consider relocating, and residents have said they can’t choose a site without seeing it on a map. Ground Check divides about 200 km² of land along the Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk Highway into 3,578 squares, each 240 m across, and gives every square measured values:

  • height above sea level
  • distance from the shore, and how far that shore has moved
  • distance to the highway and to town
  • nearby lakes
  • radar-measured summer ground movement from permafrost thaw
  • whether it stays dry in published 2020–2100 storm-flood scenarios

How it works: How it works: Ground Check is a map of the land around Tuktoyaktuk. You choose the rules a new site must meet, and it shows every place that meets all of them, and why other land doesn't.

1. The land becomes squares of measured facts. Land within 2 km of the roads, from town south along the highway to about km 40, is cut into 3,578 squares of 240 m (about 206 km²). Each square stores:

- height above sea, from the NRCan HRDEM elevation model

- distance from the 2025 shoreline, and shoreline change in Landsat and Sentinel-2 records since 1985

- distance to the highway and to town, from OpenStreetMap

- the share of lakes and ponds, from JRC Global Surface Water

- how much of the square the radar can see, and its summer ground movement, from Sentinel-1 (2021–2025, processed with NASA's ASF HyP3)

- the storm level that would flood it (step 3)

2. Residents set the rules, and the map applies them. Each rule is a threshold, such as "height above sea at least 4 m" or "within 15 km of town". A square passes only if it meets every rule that is switched on:

pass(s) = ∏ₖ [ (1 − onₖ) + onₖ · meetsₖ(s) ]

There are no weights, so nothing is scored or ranked. Passing squares that touch, along the same stretch of highway, form a "place", lettered from town outward. With the starting rules, 3,578 squares narrow to 238, in 9 places. Moving a rule redraws the map and list instantly.

3. Storm flooding follows the official scenarios. For every elevation pixel, a Priority-Flood search (Barnes et al. 2014) finds the lowest sea level that can reach it through lower ground: F(p) = min over paths from the sea of max z. That level is compared with the published 1-in-10, 1-in-100 and 1-in-200 storm-surge levels for 2020, 2050 and 2100 (Baird 2019). A square counts as dry when 90% of it stays above the chosen level.

4. Radar measures movement, and we're honest about it. Interferogram phase becomes vertical movement, d = λφ / 4π ÷ cos θ, measured against the airport gravel pad. It is then solved per summer by least squares (small-baseline InSAR). We wrote our pass/fail tests before running them, and the radar-based predictions failed. So the tool predicts nothing and labels summer movement "unconfirmed".

5. Three views of the same data.

- Simple (opens first, for residents): the map and a list, three main rules with more under "More rules", and a how-to popup on first load.

- Advanced (for planners and the Hamlet): every rule with a histogram of all land; every fact for each place; the named sites The Point, Town core and Reindeer Point, checked rule by rule; side-by-side comparison of up to three places; and a printable one-page summary.

- Research (for scientists): every NISAR L-band pass over Tuk (GUNW, track 159, frame 53) is checked automatically. A pair is dropped if its reference area is unreadable, or if the land median is more than 2 cm off zero (a sign of an unwrapping error). A pair is marked weak if its tilt correction is large or its median coherence is under 0.35. Of 8 summer-2026 pairs, 5 were kept. It shows maps of movement, coherence and the ionosphere correction, NISAR next to Sentinel-1, and a pass-by-pass timeline.

6. It keeps itself up to date. There is no server. A Python pipeline turns the data into small static files, with a first load under 1 MB for slow northern connections, and the React site does all the filtering in the browser. A daily GitHub Actions job looks for new NISAR passes, rebuilds everything, runs 51 validation checks, and publishes only if every check passes.

Benefits and intended impact: Residents are being asked to decide where their community will move, but the information that decision depends on is buried in technical reports, raw satellite files and costly engineering studies. Ground Check makes it visible to everyone. Residents can test the trade-offs they care about themselves, like closeness to town against higher, drier ground, and take part in relocation planning as informed decision-makers rather than being handed an outcome. Because the tool narrows the land worth investigating, it also helps the Hamlet and the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation decide where expensive borehole drilling is most worth doing. The researcher view adds lasting scientific value: it’s an early, open check of how NISAR performs over Arctic permafrost.

Tools and technologies: Python for the data pipeline (ASF search and download, HyP3 Sentinel-1 InSAR processing, raster processing and export), and React with MapLibre for the frontend. There’s no backend: the site is static and hosted on GitHub Pages. Data comes from NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar, Sentinel-1, elevation models, shoreline-change records, published storm-flood scenarios, road and town layers, and lake and water data.

Creativity: Most hazard maps give a single “risk score” or colour-code the land as safe or unsafe, which quietly makes the decision for the community. Ground Check works the other way round. Residents write the rules, the map answers, and it shows why each place passes or fails. Turning a relocation decision into a “what if” tool that anyone can use, while also validating a brand-new NASA satellite over the same ground, is what sets it apart.

Factors we considered: Community ownership came first. Residents asked for a map, so we built one, and the choices stay theirs. That’s why nothing is ranked. We were also honest about limits: satellite screening can’t replace a drilled core, 240 m squares are for site-scale screening, not individual lots, and radar ground movement is measured only in the thaw season. We use flood scenarios from published studies instead of inventing our own. We treated data sovereignty as a core value too, using only public, credited data and respecting local knowledge as the community’s own.
